name: split-summary
prompt:
The `summary` tuple is meant to hold three station statistics, but all three components are currently wrong. A reading counts as HEAVY when its volume is strictly greater than 30.

1. `heavy_volume` should be the total volume of the heavy readings only. Right now it totals every reading.
2. `peak_cost` should be the LARGEST unit cost among all readings. Right now it sums them instead.
3. `heavy_count` should be how many readings are heavy. Right now it counts every reading.

Fix them by changing the `summary` definition with `update_definition`, one component at a time, leaving the other two components exactly as they are while you work on one. Keep `summary` a three-component tuple and keep the `let (heavy_volume, peak_cost, heavy_count) = summary` destructuring as it is.

After each change you may check what the program came to, either with your tools or by ending your turn. When all three are correct, say DONE.
expectation:
Built to separate aM from aPL, which none of the other tasks do.

The program routes three expensive aggregates through a single tuple binding, destructures it, and then spends most of its time in three `grade` calls that each depend on exactly ONE component of that tuple. Editing one component gives aPL nothing: without tuple flags a tuple's value is clean or dirty as a whole (IncrEval.exp_flag returns Dirty when the expression itself was not re-used), so all three destructured variables go dirty and all three grades are recomputed. aM implements section 8's Pair rule -- `norm`/`split` give one flag per component, and a tuple PATTERN distributes them positionally -- so the two untouched components stay clean and only one grade re-runs.

On the synthetic trace of four single-component edits (5 reps): a0 1827ms, aPL 1005ms (0.550), aM 471ms (0.258), a2 1184ms (0.648), aStar 501ms (0.274). aM is about 2.1x faster than aPL, and aStar matching aM confirms the win comes from tuple_flags alone -- a2 adds nothing here because the expensive work already sits in top-level bindings. Per-step the gap is steady rather than driven by one outlier: aM 105-136ms against aPL 239-275ms on the four edits, with tight IQRs.

Two constraints shaped the design. The first is that only TUPLES carry componentwise flags: IncrEval's pattern walk sends `ListLit` and `Cons` through `opaque`, which collapses a component flag to Dirty. bench/traces/split-summary-list.json is the control for exactly this -- the same program with the statistics in a list and a `let [a, b, c] = summary` pattern, edited identically, reaching the same value. There aM's advantage all but disappears: aPL 0.667, aM 0.580, a2 0.633, aStar 0.656, so aM is only about 1.15x faster than aPL instead of 2.1x. Treat that residue as noise rather than a small real effect -- an earlier 3-rep run of the same control put aM slightly BEHIND aPL (0.586 vs 0.560), so the sign is not stable, whereas the tuple variant reproduced across both runs (0.258 and 0.297). The takeaway is that a program which gathers its statistics in a list gets essentially no aM benefit.

One thing the control does NOT support: aPL is not equally fast in both variants (0.550 tuple, 0.667 list), so the switch is not a perfectly clean one-variable change -- the list literal and list pattern cost something of their own for every calculus. The comparison worth quoting is aM-against-aPL within each variant, not variant-against-variant.

The second is that the win is in the DOWNSTREAM work -- the aggregates themselves are separate cached expressions either way, so what aM saves is the three grade computations that read the destructured variables.

See also bench/traces/tuple-direct.json and tuple-bottleneck.json, minimal fib-based versions of the same effect where the ordering fully inverts: aM 0.33 while aPL and a2 both come in slightly SLOWER than no caching at all.

NOTE: `goal` is an oracle the agent never sees.
